question: Apply Round Robin Scheduling Algorithm with time quantum of 3 and draw a Gantt Chart for the following set of processes and compute the average turnaround time, average wait time, average response time and the system throughput. Consider the context switch time to be negligible. Process Set(Process id, Arrival Time, CPU Burst) = {(P1, 3, 25),(P2, 2, 30),(P3, 1, 15),(P4, 0, 5)}
groundTruth: PARTIAL COVERAGE. Verbatim exam question (CSL 207 End Sem 2023-24 Q1(a)). The material has the Round Robin method with a worked Gantt chart (p.9), the time formulas (p.8) and throughput (p.7), but not this process set.

question: Assume three processes: P1, P2 and P3 existing in a system. Times taken of execution of different processes are as follows: P1 = 10 ms, P2 = 7 ms and P3 = 15 ms. The processes are executing in a sequential manner such that P1 executes first, then P2, then P3, then again P1, P2 and P3, and so on, until a process completes its execution. Assume after 3ms the CPU switches from one process to another. Pictorially using process control block (PCB), explain how context switching is done.
groundTruth: PARTIAL COVERAGE. Verbatim exam question (CSL 207 Sessional 1 2023-24 Q2). The material covers the dispatcher switching context (p.6) and time-sliced Round Robin with context switches (p.9); the PCB is not covered.

question: On early computers, every byte of data read or written was handled by the CPU (there was no DMA). What implications does this have for multiprogramming?
groundTruth: PARTIAL COVERAGE. Verbatim exam question (CSL 207 Sessional 1 2023-24 Q1(a)). The material says multiprogramming aims at maximum CPU utilisation by switching the CPU among processes (p.2); DMA is not covered.

question: On a system a totally CPU-bound process requires 50 seconds to execute. First a time quantum of 5 is given and at second time the time quantum doubles, how many times will the job be interrupted? Justify the answer with reason and a queuing diagram.
groundTruth: PARTIAL COVERAGE. Verbatim exam question (CSL 207 End Sem re-exam 2023-24 Q1(b)). Time slices / Round Robin (p.9) and CPU-bound processes (pp.3-4) are covered; the doubling-quantum scheme is not.

question: Once the OS has decided which process runs next, which module gives that process control of the CPU?
groundTruth: The dispatcher: it switches context, switches to user mode and jumps to the proper location in the user program.

question: What is the difference between throughput and turnaround time?
groundTruth: Throughput is the number of processes that complete their execution per time unit; turnaround time is the amount of time to execute a particular process.

question: Why keep several programs in memory at the same time instead of running them one at a time?
groundTruth: Multiprogramming: switching the CPU among processes gives maximum CPU utilisation.

question: In the graph of CPU burst durations, are short bursts or long bursts more common?
groundTruth: Short bursts. The frequency curve peaks (about 155) at a burst of 1-2 ms, falls to about 30 near 4 ms and stays near 0 from 8 ms to 40 ms.

question: Which type of process could do with a lower priority, and what kind of programs are examples of it?
groundTruth: CPU-bound processes (hardly any I/O, mostly CPU activity, long CPU bursts), e.g. gcc, scientific modeling, 3D rendering. Page 4 is image-only.

question: Which event moves a process from the new state into the ready state?
groundTruth: Admitted (new -> ready) in the process state diagram.

question: According to the state diagram, what happens to a running process when an interrupt occurs?
groundTruth: It goes back to the ready state (running -> ready on interrupt).

question: bhai turnaround time aur waiting time ka formula kya hai?
groundTruth: Turnaround time = burst time + waiting time; waiting time = turnaround time - burst time.

question: wat is dispach latncy
groundTruth: The time it takes for the dispatcher to stop one process and start another running.

question: How many context switches are there in the round robin worked example?
groundTruth: 7 context switches (schedule P1 P2 P3 P4 P1 P2 P4 P1).

question: What does response time measure, and how do you compute it for a process?
groundTruth: The time from submission of a request until the first response is produced (p.7); response time = time the process first gets the CPU - arrival time (p.8).

question: In the video, where does the scheduler choose the next process from?
groundTruth: From the processes in the ready queue ('The Waiting Room' box of the How Scheduling Works slide).

question: What does the video say the choice of scheduling algorithm affects?
groundTruth: System fairness and responsiveness ('The Impact' box).

question: What is the goal of CPU scheduling according to the video?
groundTruth: Maximize CPU utilization and optimize system performance ('The Goal' box).

question: Which everyday situation does the video use as an analogy for CPU scheduling?
groundTruth: A service counter: a clerk serving a line of waiting customers.

question: In the video's analogy, what does the rule for choosing the next customer stand for?
groundTruth: The CPU scheduling policy.
